name: Timur
info: Timur, or Tamerlane, a Turco-Mongol conqueror of the Barlas tribe who founded the Timurid Empire in the late 14th century, campaigning from Delhi to Anatolia with great slaughter while patronising scholars and building up Samarkand.

facts.born: in the 1320s, near Kesh (now Shahrisabz, Uzbekistan) in the Chagatai Khanate; son of Taraghai, a noble of the Turkicised Mongol Barlas tribe; later Timurid histories give 8 April 1336
facts.died: 17 or 18 February 1405, at Farab beyond the Syr Darya, of illness during a winter campaign against Ming China; buried in the Gur-e-Amir, Samarkand
facts.role: Chief of the Barlas from about 1360; sovereign at Balkh from about 1370, ruling as amir and güregen (royal son-in-law) in the name of puppet Chagatayid khans; styled Sahib Qiran, 'Lord of the Conjunction'
facts.known: founding the Timurid Empire; wars with Tokhtamysh and the Golden Horde; the sack of Delhi (1398); the sacks of Isfahan, Baghdad, Aleppo and Damascus; the defeat of Bayezid I at Ankara (1402); patronage of Samarkand and of scholars; the Timurid Renaissance

t: Timur rose from a minor Barlas noble to master of the western Chagatai Khanate by about 1370 and spent the next 35 years at war, defeating the Golden Horde, the Delhi Sultanate, the Mamluks and the Ottomans.
His campaigns relied on terror: Isfahan, Delhi, Baghdad and Damascus were massacred, and scholars estimate that his wars caused the deaths of millions of people.
He enriched Samarkand and patronised scholars and poets, but his empire fragmented soon after his death; his descendants included Ulugh Beg and Babur, founder of the Mughal Empire.
dyk: Timur's nickname, Temur-i Lang, 'Timur the Lame', from injuries to his right leg and hand, is the origin of the Western name Tamerlane; a Soviet examination of his remains in 1941 confirmed the injuries.
ev: Timur defeats his rival Amir Husayn and is proclaimed sovereign at Balkh
Timur begins his conquest of Persia with the destruction of Herat
After a revolt, Timur orders the massacre of the people of Isfahan
Timur defeats Tokhtamysh at the Battle of the Terek River
Timur invades northern India and sacks Delhi
Timur's armies sack Damascus and Baghdad
Timur defeats and captures the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I at the Battle of Ankara
Timur dies at Farab on campaign against Ming China

sections.early:
Timur was born near Kesh, now Shahrisabz in Uzbekistan, some 80 kilometres south of Samarkand, in what was then the Chagatai Khanate. Later Timurid histories give his birth as 8 April 1336, but most sources from his lifetime point to the late 1320s, and several scholars suspect the later date was chosen to link him to the last Ilkhan, Abu Sa'id, who died in 1336. His name means 'iron' in Chagatai, his mother tongue.

He belonged to the Barlas, a Mongol tribe that had become Turkicised in many ways and whose members had served the Chinggisid rulers since the 13th century. Historian Peter Jackson considers his Mongol ancestry generally accepted; Timurid histories trace his father's line to a male-line ancestor of Genghis Khan, though no evidence from his lifetime makes the link directly. His father Taraghai is described as a minor noble, but Beatrice Forbes Manz argues that Timur may later have understated his father's standing. The origins of his mother, Tekina Khatun, are unclear and the sources disagree.

As a youth he led a small band raiding travellers for animals. Around 1363, it is believed, he was shot by two arrows, in the right leg and the right hand, losing two fingers, either while stealing a sheep or, as some believe, while serving as a mercenary in Sistan. The injuries disabled him for life and gave him the Persian nickname Temur-i Lang, 'Timur the Lame', the source of 'Tamerlane'.
sections.rise:
By about 1360 Timur had become a military leader of Turkic tribesmen. He allied himself with the amir Qazaghan and led a thousand horsemen into Khorasan. After Qazaghan's murder, the eastern Chagatai khan Tughlugh Timur invaded; Timur, sent to negotiate, joined him instead and was rewarded with Transoxiana. Around this time his father died, on 12 March 1360 by the Zafarnama's account, and Timur became chief of the Barlas. When Tughlugh tried to set his son Ilyas Khoja over Transoxiana, Timur repelled the invasion with a smaller force.

He and his brother-in-law Amir Husayn, at first fellow fugitives, became rivals. Timur won followers at Balkh among merchants, tribesmen, clergy and farmers by sharing his belongings, while Husayn alienated them with heavy taxes. Around 1370 Husayn surrendered and was later assassinated, and Timur was proclaimed sovereign at Balkh. He married Husayn's wife Saray Mulk Khanum, a descendant of Genghis Khan.

By Mongol tradition only a descendant of Genghis Khan could be khan, so Timur ruled as amir in the name of a puppet khan, Suyurghatmish, and took the title güregen, 'royal son-in-law'. He could not be caliph either, and instead styled himself Sahib Qiran, 'Lord of the Conjunction', a title that A. Azfar Moin calls messianic, and presented himself as a spiritual descendant of Ali.
sections.deeds:
Timur spent 35 years at war. From 1383 he conquered Persia, then divided among several dynasties after the Ilkhanate's collapse, destroying Herat when it would not surrender, taking Tabriz in 1386 and Shiraz in 1393, when the Muzaffarids were annexed. In August 1393 he took Baghdad by surprise after a march of eight days from Shiraz. He fought his former protégé Tokhtamysh, khan of the Golden Horde, leading over 100,000 men deep into the steppe to win at the Kondurcha River in 1391 and defeating him finally at the Terek River in 1395. His armies destroyed Sarai and Astrakhan, and the Golden Horde never recovered.

In 1398 he crossed the Indus with 90,000 men into the declining Delhi Sultanate. On 17 December he defeated Sultan Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah Tughluq before Delhi, sending burning camels against the sultan's war elephants, and sacked one of the richest cities in the world.

From 1399 he fought the Ottoman sultan Bayezid I and the Mamluks. He conquered Tiflis, sacked Sivas, Aleppo and Damascus, and took Baghdad again in June 1401. On 20 July 1402 he defeated and captured Bayezid at the Battle of Ankara, opening the twelve-year Ottoman Interregnum, and in December took Smyrna from the Knights Hospitallers. He ruled his core lands in Central Asia and Iran through a centralised administration that joined Turko-Mongol traditions to a Persian bureaucracy, and brought scholars and artisans to Samarkand.
sections.opponents:
Timur's wars were waged with deliberate terror. When Isfahan revolted against his taxes in 1387 he ordered its people massacred; the death toll is reckoned at between 100,000 and 200,000, and an eyewitness counted more than 28 towers of about 1,500 heads each. Herat was left in ruins, and prisoners at Isfizar were cemented alive into the walls. Before the battle at Delhi he had some 100,000 captive slaves killed for fear they would revolt; the city was sacked, its people enslaved and, after an uprising, massacred, and Delhi did not recover for almost a century. At Baghdad in 1401, 20,000 people were killed, every soldier being ordered to bring back two severed heads. In Armenia and Georgia more than 60,000 people were taken as slaves. Scholars estimate that his campaigns caused the deaths of millions; Khwarazm, which repeatedly rose against him, suffered most.

His main enemies were Muslim states, whose rulers and theologians accused him of unbelief. Ibn Arabshah wrote that he preferred the laws of Genghis Khan and that many theologians declared him an unbeliever; the Ottomans called his army 'worse than the infidels', and Russian chronicles portrayed him as an evil pagan. He attacked the Ismailis of Anjudan in 1393. The Tatar historian Şihabetdin Märcani quoted the judgement that Timur did Islam many times more harm than Genghis Khan or Hulagu.

The sources are divided: William Jones contrasted the Timurid Zafarnamas' 'benevolent and illustrious prince' with Arabshah's 'deformed and impious' tyrant.
sections.last:
After Ankara, Bayezid died in captivity, and his son Mehmed Çelebi acted as Timur's vassal, minting coins with Timur's name beside his own. When Qara Yusuf took Baghdad in 1402, Timur sent his grandson Abu Bakr to retake it. He then passed through Ardabil, where he gave captives to Ali Safavi, leader of the Safaviyya, and returned by way of Khorasan to Samarkand, where he spent nine months celebrating and preparing to invade Mongolia and China. In Samarkand he received the Castilian embassy of Ruy González de Clavijo in 1403–1406, and he corresponded with Charles VI of France.

He had refused the Ming emperors' claims to treat him as a subject, detaining their envoys. In December 1404, though he usually fought in spring, he set out on a winter campaign against Ming China. He fell ill in camp beyond the Syr Darya and died at Farab on 17 or 18 February 1405, before reaching the Chinese border. His body was embalmed and taken to Samarkand, where it lies in the Gur-e-Amir.

He had outlived both his chosen heirs: his son Jahangir, who died in 1376, and his grandson Muhammad Sultan, who died of battle wounds in 1403. Only on his deathbed did he name Muhammad Sultan's younger brother Pir Muhammad, who could not win enough support. A bitter civil war followed among his descendants until his youngest son, Shah Rukh, took the throne in 1409.
sections.legacy:
Timur's legacy is mixed. Central Asia flourished under him and he keeps a positive image there, while he is vilified by many in Arabia, Iraq, Persia and India, where some of his greatest atrocities took place. Ibn Khaldun, who met him at Damascus in 1401, praised him for uniting much of the Muslim world. Beatrice Forbes Manz sees his career as the last manifestation of the military power of the nomads, and his empire set the stage for the gunpowder empires of the 16th and 17th centuries. Beyond Iran he plundered and neglected the lands he conquered, which may have helped his empire break up after his death. Nader Shah later almost re-enacted his campaigns.

His reign led to the Timurid Renaissance. Persian became the main language of administration and literature across his lands, while a literary Chagatai Turkic came into use beside it. His grandson Ulugh Beg ruled Central Asia as an astronomer-sultan, and his descendant Babur founded the Mughal Empire. His campaigns also virtually exterminated the Church of the East, which was afterwards confined largely to a small area now called the Assyrian Triangle, and his wars hastened the breakup of the Golden Horde, which let Moscow rise.

In Uzbekistan he is called the 'Founder of the Uzbek nation', and his monument in Tashkent stands where Karl Marx's statue once did. In Europe he became a figure of drama and opera, from Christopher Marlowe's Tamburlaine to Handel's Tamerlano. The supposed autobiography, the Malfuzat-i Timuri, is almost certainly a 17th-century fabrication.

summary: Timur, or Tamerlane, rose from a minor Barlas noble to found the Timurid Empire, defeating the Golden Horde, the Delhi Sultanate, the Mamluks and the Ottomans between about 1370 and 1405. His conquests killed millions and wrecked cities from Delhi to Baghdad, while Samarkand flourished and his heirs led the Timurid Renaissance and founded the Mughal Empire.
